Coney
KOH-nee
n.
Middle English conig from Old French conin, from Latin cuniculus, “rabbit.” In the KJV, however, the word translates the Hebrew shāphān, which most modern scholars identify as the rock hyrax (Procavia capensis), a small mammal of Sinai and the Holy Land, not the European rabbit.

📖 Biblical Definition

The coney in the KJV is the small mammal called in modern English the rock hyrax—a furry, rodent-looking creature of approximately rabbit size that lives in colonies among the rocks of Sinai, Arabia, and the Holy Land. The KJV translators rendered the Hebrew shāphān as coney (a Middle English word that originally meant rabbit) because no European reader of the early 1600s would have known the rock hyrax by name; the rabbit was the closest familiar approximation. The coney appears four times in the Old Testament. Twice in the lists of unclean animals: and the coney, because he cheweth the cud, but divideth not the hoof; he is unclean unto you (Lev 11:5; cf. Deut 14:7). The coney’s ruminant-style chewing motion (it chews and re-chews its food in a way that resembles cud-chewing without being technically the same process) and its lack of cloven hoofs put it in the unclean category of animals Israel was forbidden to eat. Twice in the wisdom literature, however, the coney appears in a different register: the high hills are a refuge for the wild goats; and the rocks for the conies (Ps 104:18); and most strikingly, the conies are but a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks (Prov 30:26). The Proverbs reference is the one with the deepest pastoral application. The coney is named as one of four things which are little upon the earth, but they are exceeding wise (Prov 30:24-28): the ants, the conies, the locusts, and the spider. The coney’s wisdom is precisely its self-knowledge: it is a feeble creature, defenseless against predators, with no speed, no claws, no horns—and it has wisely chosen to dwell in the rocks where its weakness is compensated by the inaccessibility of its refuge. The application to the saint is direct. The saint is a feeble creature (Ps 103:14: he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust), defenseless in himself against the spiritual predators arrayed against him, with no native strength against the powers of darkness. Like the coney, he is wise to make his house in the Rock—the Rock who is Christ (1 Cor 10:4), the Rock of his salvation (Deut 32:15; 2 Sam 22:47; Ps 18:46), the Rock higher than I (Ps 61:2). The feeble folk who dwell in the Rock is the picture of every saint in every generation: weak in himself, strong in his refuge, made wise by his honest assessment of his own weakness and his deliberate flight to the Rock that is stronger than every assault.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines CONEY as a rabbit; in the KJV, however, used for the Hebrew shāphān, which is the rock hyrax of Sinai and the Holy Land; biblically significant as one of Proverbs 30’s four wise feeble things, the feeble folk who make their houses in the rocks.

CONEY, n. — A rabbit; in scripture (KJV), the rock hyrax (shāphān), a small mammal of the Holy Land. The conies are but a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks (Prov 30:26).

ROCK, n. — A large mass of stony matter, usually compounded of two or more simple minerals. In scripture, often used as a figure of the LORD as the firm support and refuge of His people (Deut 32:4; Ps 18:2; 1 Cor 10:4).

📖 Key Scripture

Proverbs 30:24-26 — "There be four things which are little upon the earth, but they are exceeding wise: The ants are a people not strong, yet they prepare their meat in the summer; The conies are but a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks."

Psalm 104:18 — "The high hills are a refuge for the wild goats; and the rocks for the conies."

Leviticus 11:5 — "And the coney, because he cheweth the cud, but divideth not the hoof; he is unclean unto you."

Psalm 18:2 — "The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; my God, my strength, in whom I will trust; my buckler, and the horn of my salvation, and my high tower."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The coney-doctrine is corrupted chiefly by being overlooked altogether—a minor zoological detail in the dietary laws and a passing wisdom-literature reference, often skipped in contemporary preaching—and by the loss of the pastoral application of Proverbs 30:26 to the saint as the feeble folk wisely dwelling in the Rock that is Christ.

expand to see more

The coney is one of many small biblical creatures (along with the spider, the locust, the ant) that contemporary preaching tends to skip past as zoological curiosities of a vanished agrarian world. Proverbs 30’s four wise feeble things are not, however, mere natural-history. They are pastoral wisdom embodied in observation: the ants’ preparation in summer for the want of winter (a parable of foresight and diligence); the conies’ choosing-of-rocks for their refuge (a parable of honest self-assessment and wise flight to a stronger refuge); the locusts’ ordered swarming without a king (a parable of cooperative unity); the spider’s skilled work in places of human power (a parable of patient skill reaching places the powerful cannot bar). Each yields pastoral substance the careful reader is meant to draw. The recovery is the recovery of the Proverbs-style observation: the natural world is full of parables the Spirit-trained eye sees, and the wisdom literature trains the saint to look and see and learn.

The supreme pastoral application of the coney specifically is to the doctrine of the saint as the feeble folk who wisely dwells in the Rock. The Bible knows no flattering doctrine of human native strength; it is candid about the creaturely weakness, the indwelling sin, the spiritual powers arrayed against the believer. The coney’s wisdom is the saint’s wisdom: honest assessment of one’s own feebleness, deliberate flight to the Rock that is Christ. The saint who has not assessed his own weakness has not yet learned what the coney teaches; the saint who has assessed his weakness and has not yet fled to the Rock is in the unguarded condition of the feeble creature exposed in the open. The recovery is the recovery of the picture: see your weakness honestly, see Christ as the Rock that is stronger than every assault, dwell in Him, find in Him the refuge no native strength could provide. The conies are but a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks—a pastoral picture worth thirty volumes of self-help on developing native strength.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shāphān (the rock hyrax; rendered coney in the KJV); appears in the dietary laws as unclean (Lev 11:5; Deut 14:7) and in the wisdom literature as the feeble folk who wisely dwells in the rocks (Ps 104:18; Prov 30:26)—the pastoral picture of the saint dwelling in the Rock that is Christ.

expand to see more

Hebrew shāphān (H8227) — rock hyrax (4 OT uses; KJV coney).

Greek petra (G4073) — rock (the great NT word for the Christ-Rock; 1 Cor 10:4; Matt 16:18).

Hebrew tsur (H6697) — rock, cliff (the OT word for the LORD as Rock; Deut 32:4; Ps 18:2).

Hebrew sela‘ (H5553) — cliff, rock (used for the conies’ refuge in Ps 104:18).
